title: The Divine Physician and the Ruler of the World
english: …by whom is he to be reproached? For Porphyry indeed writes to Nemertius: 'Because the audacity of speaking of justice to God has occurred, if it were explained, it would be found to be full of injustice, and it is found to be entirely empty.' Therefore, it is holy and blameless, and truly the judgment of God is just. To think otherwise is a disease and a crime.

Since our adversary is hostile to our words, let Porphyry be heard writing again: 'Not only does he adapt one thing to the utility of the whole and the duration of harmony, and another time to another thing, but he is also a tutor, savior, and physician of all. Did he not prescribe to physicians, according to the art he himself handed down, that for those perceiving the dangers imminent to the whole body, one must cut certain parts, others burn, others rot, and others divide, so that the whole may be saved?'

Mothers and nurses, not ignorant that this is done by a doctor so that the whole body may be saved, sometimes prevent it, wailing and crying; but the father is present and, according to his own providence, urges the doctor and, for the sake of saving the whole, takes away food from the one crying. And to the one who is well, God does not permit certain things to happen or to be separated from others, just as a finger from the whole body, for the benefit of the whole. If we were to investigate divine reasons, we would see that it is necessary to prevent certain things from being born, and to others, to give death as a gift of piety.

Although Porphyry has a remarkable divine reasoning, we must proceed nonetheless; and it seems that he fought against God's majesty before Julian, but what he sensed and what he wrote is sufficient to be proven by these things. I will add one more of his sayings to this sentiment. Chrysippus, following Socrates, did not want to say that created things were from God, saying: 'Who is a novice?' but this was his status. For if no better administration can be designated for divine matters, it must be thought that created things are as they are. For if you were called to rule in some part of the empire for the public utility, you could not serve the laws differently than if you served some by exile, others by proscription, and others by death, which would not benefit everyone.

We will not concede to the ruler of this entire world that he should govern beyond his comprehension, whether through deaths, or changes, or through the uncertainty of the ages. For indeed, a part of humanity is being managed, and we will not permit the one who holds a portion of the beginning of providence to oversee beyond the present kingdom, nor the one who is subject to the laws for the benefit of the state, nor the one who keeps the laws; and for the state which walls in some of the rulers and deprives others and even kills some, we will not permit him to govern without reproach, even though he has preserved life for all, because this is common to all. Julian presents himself as impious, insulting the divine judgments and substance, and he considers all things holy to be unholy; he attributes impiety and invokes wrath, and he transforms the virtuous into something else and places the agitated in a secure and firm position. Let us concede, as if to a doctor, that those who have been shaken may be healed; let us permit, as a physician, to cut off a small member for the sake of the salvation of the whole body.

Let us permit, as a judge of the body, to cut off a small part, having removed the wicked, to rule those subject to the laws, not to contend with the laws, but to govern with politeness. For as I have already said, the good do not associate with the wicked, but rather with one good, Phinees; a multitude of the wicked is saved, and Phinees is valued (Numbers 25:7-8). Phinees was not valued because he was pierced by a grave wound, but because, having steeled himself with a zeal for God, he more fiercely fought against the deserters with singular counsel.

It perhaps does not please Julian that necessary penalties have been instituted, for he is not unaware that he is numbered among such men. Nor will he avoid the ultimate penalty, having thrown away his shield and having been led away from these matters, being convicted; for he has fallen into the abyss of impiety, and he thinks perhaps he can oppose God's laws and transfer divine judgments, considering himself able to bear the power towards what seems right to him …
translator_notes: The text begins mid-sentence: '...a quoquam reprehendi?'
The reference to Phinees is an allusion to Numbers 25:7-8.
